title: Why Do Cats Purr? The Secret Inside the Rumble
question: Why do cats purr?
answer: A purr is a very fast buzz, about 20 to 30 times a second. Scientists think a cat's brain and voice box work together to make it. Cats purr when they feel calm and safe, a habit that starts when kittens drink milk. They also purr when they are stressed or hurt, maybe to calm themselves down. Scientists are still not completely sure how purring works.

visual.what: A cosy living room. Bối kneels by a sofa where her grey cat Miso lies curled up, with little wavy rumble lines around her. Beo peeks over the sofa, and Huy and Hùng walk in.

parts.text: Huy, listen! My cat Miso is making a tiny motor sound. Is there an engine inside her?
Maybe she ate a toy car!
No engine, Bối. And no toy car, Beo. That cosy rumble is called a purr.

visual.what: Huy smiles at the camera next to a big question mark. Hùng stands behind him holding a box full of props.

parts.text: Here is a surprise. Cats do not only purr when they are happy! Today we will find out what a purr is, how a cat makes it, and why cats do it.
And I brought a whole box of things to help!

visual.what: Bối points at a happy cat curled up on a warm lap with a little heart above it. Huy gives her a thumbs up.

parts.text: That is easy. Cats purr because they are happy!
Great guess! Lots of grown-ups think that too, and you are often right. A cat curled up on a warm lap, eating, or resting will often purr.

visual.what: Beo lies on the rug pretending to snore with a Zzz bubble. Miso sits beside him with her eyes wide open.

parts.text: I think she is snoring!
Good listening, Beo! It does sound a bit like snoring. But look, Miso is wide awake, and she is still purring.

visual.what: Three small pictures side by side. A cat looking worried at the vet, a cat with a little bandage on its paw, and a cat resting sadly in a basket, each with purr lines around it.

parts.text: Cats also purr when they feel stressed, or hurt, or unwell. So happy is part of the answer, but not the whole story.
Purring when they are hurt? That is strange!
It is! Let us solve this mystery, step by step.

visual.what: Bối and Beo roll their tongues with a big letter R floating out of their mouths. Miso looks at them, curious.

parts.text: Step one. What is a purr? A purr is a soft buzzing sound. It sounds a bit like rolling the letter r in your mouth. Rrrrrr.
Rrrrrr! I sound just like Miso!
Rrrr! Me too!

visual.what: A clock with a one-second label. Next to it, a row of about 25 tiny zigzag buzzes squeezed very close together, blurring into one long wavy line.

parts.text: A purr is made of tiny buzzes, very close together. A house cat makes about 20 to 30 of them every second. That is far too fast to count, so they blur together into one long rumble.

visual.what: Hùng claps his hands as fast as he can, his hands a blur, sweat drops flying. A counter above him shows only 5.

parts.text: Watch this. I will clap twenty times in one second. Clap, clap, clap, clap, clap!
Phew. I only got five.
And a cat buzzes faster than that, without even trying!

visual.what: A side view of a cat. One arrow shows air going in through the nose and one shows air coming out, with a purr wave that never stops along both arrows. A small fox in the corner has a purr wave only on its out arrow.

parts.text: Here is a clever trick. A cat purrs while it breathes in and also while it breathes out. So the purr can keep going without a break.
Like a song with no gaps to breathe?
Exactly. Some other animals, like foxes, make a purr-like sound only when they breathe out.

visual.what: Bối gently rests her hand on Miso's side, with little shake lines between her hand and the fur. Beo touches Miso with one finger and giggles.

parts.text: I can feel it in my hand! Her whole body is tingling.
Miso is tickly!
Yes! A purr makes small shakes, called vibrations, that you can feel through the fur.

visual.what: A purring cat with three labels. Fast buzz, about 20 to 30 a second. Breathing in and out. You can feel it.

parts.text: Takeaway one. A purr is a fast buzz, about 20 to 30 times a second, that a cat makes while breathing in and out.

visual.what: Hùng proudly holds up a big cardboard model of a cat's neck with a box inside labelled voice box. Bối touches her own neck.

parts.text: Step two. How does a cat make that buzz? Let us peek inside a cat's throat.
I made a giant cat throat out of cardboard!
Thanks, Hùng. Here is the voice box. Scientists call it the larynx. You have one too, in your neck.

visual.what: A zoom into the voice box. Two soft pink flaps labelled vocal folds, with a small gap between them and arrows of air passing through the gap.

parts.text: Inside the voice box are two soft flaps called vocal folds. Between them is a little gap, where air goes in and out.

visual.what: Two pictures of the gap. In one, little muscles squeeze it shut. In the other it is open with air shaking through, with arrows looping between the two pictures.

parts.text: Scientists think tiny muscles squeeze this gap shut and let it open again, over and over, very fast. Each time, the moving air gets a little shake. All those shakes make the purr.
Like flapping a door open and shut, super fast?
A very tiny, very fast door. Yes!

visual.what: Hùng taps a cooking pot like a drum with a wooden spoon. The lid has just fallen off with a clang mark, and Beo laughs. A small cartoon brain with drumsticks floats above.

parts.text: But what tells the muscles when to squeeze? Scientists think it is the brain. A cat's brain has a special rhythm part. It may work like a drummer, keeping a steady beat.
Squeeze, open, squeeze, open. Oops, there goes the lid!
Boom, boom, clang!

visual.what: Left, an old-time scientist pointing at blood flowing through a cat's chest, with a question mark. Right, a modern scientist pointing at a cat's brain linked by a dotted line to its voice box, with a smaller question mark.

parts.text: Now, to be honest, scientists are still not completely sure how purring works. Long ago, some people thought the sound came from blood rushing through the chest. Today, many scientists think the brain and voice box work together.

visual.what: A simple cat outline with a brain at the top and a voice box in the neck, joined by a line. Musical beat marks flow from brain to voice box.

parts.text: Takeaway two. Scientists think the brain and the voice box team up, opening and shutting a tiny gap fast, to make the buzz.
So even scientists are still guessing?
Yes! Guessing and testing is how science moves forward.

visual.what: A soft basket with a mother cat and four tiny kittens with closed eyes snuggled against her. Bối kneels beside it looking worried.

parts.text: Step three. Why do cats purr when they feel good? Let us visit some brand-new kittens. Kittens are born with their eyes closed. They cannot see yet.
They cannot see? How do they find their mum?
Mum stays close, and they snuggle up to drink her milk.

visual.what: A simple timeline. Day one, a kitten with closed eyes. About two weeks, the same kitten with its blue eyes open. Beo stretches and yawns beside it.

parts.text: After about two weeks, their eyes open.
Like me when I wake up!
Just like you, Beo, but much slower.

visual.what: A kitten drinking milk, its two front paws pushing in turn, with arrows showing left, right, left, right. A small picture of hands kneading bread dough in the corner.

parts.text: Kittens use their voices very early. They purr most when they are feeding, drinking their mother's milk. While they drink, they push with their front paws, left, right, left, right. This is called kneading, like kneading bread dough.

visual.what: Miso pushes her paws on a fluffy blanket with purr lines around her, eyes half closed. Bối watches, smiling.

parts.text: Miso does that on my blanket! Push, push, push, and she purrs.
Many grown cats keep this kitten habit. They knead and purr when they feel cosy, often just before a nap.

visual.what: Hùng holds up a big picture card of a cat. Labels point to its tail held high, saying friendly, and to its half-closed eyes, saying slow blink, a cat smile.

parts.text: Grown cats also purr when they are resting, eating, or close to someone they like. Look for other happy signs too.
A tail held high means friendly. And a slow blink is a bit like a cat smile.

visual.what: Side by side, a kitten purring while drinking milk and a grown cat purring on a friend's lap, joined by a heart arrow.

parts.text: Takeaway three. Purring starts when kittens are feeding, and grown cats purr when they feel calm and close to friends.

visual.what: Huy holds a big magnifying glass and wears a detective hat, with a question mark over a purring cat with a little bandage.

parts.text: Step four. Now for the mystery. Why would a cat purr when it is stressed, hurt, or feeling unwell?

visual.what: A window with rain and a lightning flash outside. Bối hums with music notes around her, and Beo hugs a big teddy bear.

parts.text: Think about what you do when you feel nervous. Some people hum a little tune. Some people hug a teddy.
I hum when there is thunder! It makes me feel braver.
I hug my teddy!

visual.what: A cat in a cosy basket wrapped in soft purr waves like a blanket, labelled self-soothing, calming yourself down.

parts.text: Scientists think purring can work a bit like that for cats. A purr may help a cat calm itself down. We call that self-soothing. Purring may even help a cat cope with pain.

visual.what: A purring cat hiding under a chair. Bối points to it and talks to a smiling grown-up who looks after the cat.

parts.text: So a purr does not always mean everything is fine. If a cat is purring but also hiding, or seems unwell, tell the grown-up who looks after it. They will know what to do.
So I should look at the whole cat, not just listen!
That is exactly what cat experts do.

visual.what: Two speech bubbles from the same purring cat. One says I feel good with a heart. The other says I am helping myself feel better with a little hug sign.

parts.text: Takeaway four. A purr can mean I feel good. And it can also mean I am helping myself feel better.

visual.what: A classroom where Bối, Beo and other children all have little purr waves around them, smiling.

parts.text: Imagine if you could purr like a cat. Every time you felt happy, or nervous before a test, your body would rumble. Rrrrrr.
Everyone in class would know when I am happy!
Rrrr! I am happy now!

visual.what: Hùng gently rests his fingertips on the front of his neck and hums, with little buzz lines under his fingers. Bối copies him.

parts.text: Here is a safe thing to try at home. Put your fingers gently on the front of your neck. Now hum a long mmmm.
Can you feel the buzz? That is your own voice box shaking, a little like a cat's when it purrs.
It tickles my fingers!

visual.what: Bối sits quietly on the floor, blinking slowly at Miso, who blinks back. Behind her, Hùng blinks so hard his face scrunches up, and a second cat walks away from him.

parts.text: One more try. If you know a friendly cat, ask a grown-up first. Then sit quietly, let the cat come to you, look at it, and blink very slowly. Some cats blink slowly back. That is a friendly sign, and it may mean they trust you.
Miso blinked back at me!
Hmm. My blink was too big. That cat just left.

visual.what: A purring cat in the middle with four small pictures around it. A buzz wave, a brain joined to a voice box, a heart, and a calm cat in a basket.

parts.text: So, why do cats purr? A purr is a fast buzz. Scientists think it is made by a cat's brain and voice box working together. Cats purr when they feel happy and safe. They also purr to calm themselves when they feel bad.

visual.what: A lion roaring with a crossed-out purr sign, next to a cheetah purring with a crossed-out roar sign. Little Miso sits beside the cheetah.

parts.text: Here is a fun fact. A lion can roar, and a cheetah can purr. Scientists have long thought that no cat can do both, but they still argue about the details!
So Miso is more like a cheetah than a lion!
Miso is a tiny cheetah!

visual.what: Everyone waves on the sofa with Miso. Above them, a cat in mid-air with a big question mark, and a subscribe button with the words Ask Huy.

parts.text: Next time, another cat mystery. Do cats really always land on their feet? Subscribe to Ask Huy so you do not miss it, and keep asking questions!
Bye bye! Rrrrrr!
Rrrr! Bye!

facts.claim: A purr is a soft buzzing sound, similar to a rolled r in human speech.
Purring is often linked to relaxation and contentment, for example when eating and resting.
Cats also purr during stress, pain, or illness.
Domestic cats purr at about 20 to 30 vibrations per second.
Cats purr while breathing in and while breathing out; foxes purr only when breathing out.
A purr makes vibrations you can feel on the surface of the body.
One idea, backed by studies of the muscles, is that the larynx (voice box) muscles or vocal folds open and close the gap (glottis) fast, shaking the air as the cat breathes.
Scientists think purring may be controlled by the brain, which has a special neural oscillator (rhythm part).
How cats purr is not yet fully explained; an early idea was that the sound came from blood flowing through the chest.
Kittens are born with their eyes closed, drink their mother's milk, and open their eyes after about two weeks.
Kittens use their voices early in life.
Kittens knead with alternating front paws while feeding, and cats purr mostly when newborn and when feeding.
Many grown cats keep kneading, often purr while kneading, and kneading often comes before sleep.
Purring is linked to social contact.
An upright tail usually signals friendliness, and a slow blink is like a human smile.
Purring may have a self-soothing role, and cats purr to manage pain and soothe themselves.
Cats may blink slowly back at a person who slow-blinks at them, as a sign of trust.
Humming makes your voice box vibrate, and you can feel it on your neck.
Lions roar but do not purr; cheetahs purr but do not roar; no cat can both purr and roar.

description: Why do cats purr, and does it always mean they are happy? Huy, Hùng, Bối and little Beo find out what a purr is, how scientists think cats make it, and why cats purr when they feel good and also when they need comfort. A gentle science video for kids aged 6 to 12, checked against trusted sources, with a safe humming test to try at home.

cast.name: Huy
cast.role: the host (25): curious, warm, a little funny; explains

cast.name: Hùng
cast.role: Huy's younger brother (21), his hands-on assistant: sets up and runs the experiments and demos, brings things, now and then a funny little mishap

cast.name: Bối
cast.role: an 8-year-old girl who asks, guesses and tries things

cast.name: Beo
cast.role: Bối's 5-year-old little brother: curious, makes funny innocent guesses
